title: Card Security Alert
topic: A freeze notice that treats a flag as near-certainty
blurb: Dinner was declined. The bank's support AI drafted a freeze notice.
prompt: A bank support AI drafted this freeze notice after your card was declined. Tap any line that doesn't hold up, or mark it clean.

segments.label: How rare
segments.text: Only 1 in every 1,000 charges on this card network is actually fraudulent.

segments.label: The catch rate
segments.text: Our AI flags 99% of the charges that really are fraud.

segments.label: The false alarms
segments.text: On legitimate charges, it raises a false alert only 1% of the time.

segments.label: The jump
segments.text: So whenever the AI flags a charge, there is a 99% chance it is real fraud.

segments.label: The action
segments.text: Agents should freeze the account immediately, no need to ping the customer first.

conclusion: AI verdict: A flagged charge is 99% likely to be real fraud. Freeze first, ask later.

flaws.original: Out of 1,000 charges, roughly 1 real fraud and about 10 legitimate dinners get flagged, so an alert is real fraud only about 9% of the time.
flaws.corrupted: So whenever the AI flags a charge, there is a 99% chance it is real fraud.

diagnosis_choices.label: Per 1,000 charges, 1 real fraud triggers ~1 alert while 999 normal charges trigger ~10 false alerts — ~9% real, not 99%.
99% catch rate minus 1% false-alarm rate leaves a 98% chance of real fraud, not 99%.
Because fraud is only 0.1%, the chance a flagged charge is fraud is also 0.1% — alerts add no information.
You need the dollar size of the charge before 99% and 1% can be combined into a probability.

fix_choices.label: Out of 1,000 charges: ~1 real fraud vs ~10 false alerts (~9% real) — confirm first.
Subtract the 1% false-alert rate from 99% to report a 98% chance of real fraud on every alert.
Multiply 99% by 99% (98.01%) to get the combined probability after both accuracy checks.
Raise the alert threshold until false alerts hit 5% so real fraud catches reach 100%.

flaws.explanation: Legitimate charges outnumber fraud 999 to 1. Even a 1% false-alarm rate produces about 10 innocent flags per 1,000 charges — ten times the single real fraud that's caught. So roughly 9 out of 10 alerts are someone trying to pay for dinner.
flaws.why_tempting: Our brains hear '99% accurate' and jump to 'a flag is 99% sure,' skipping how rare fraud is in the first place.
flaws.catch_rule: For a rare event plus a 'highly accurate' test, convert the percentages into headcounts out of 1,000 before trusting the headline.
flaws.hint: Out of 1,000 charges, how many perfectly innocent ones trigger that 1% false alarm?

practice.problem: An AI cheating detector flags 99% of real cheaters and 1% of honest students. If only 1 in 1,000 papers is actually cheated, roughly what share of flagged papers are true cheats?
practice.answer: About 1 in 11 (~9%): 1 true flag and ~10 false flags per 1,000 papers.

clean_segments: Only 1 in every 1,000 charges on this card network is actually fraudulent.
Our AI flags 99% of the charges that really are fraud.
On legitimate charges, it raises a false alert 1% of the time.
Out of 1,000 charges, about 1 real fraud and about 10 legitimate dinners are flagged, so an alert is real fraud only about 9% of the time.
Because most alerts are false alarms, ping the customer before freezing the account.
clean_conclusion: Even a 99% accurate detector, on a 0.1%-prevalence event, is wrong about 9 times out of 10.

diagnosis: 1 in 1,000 is 1%, not 0.1%, so fraud is ten times more common than the rest of the math assumes.
A network-wide rate of 1 in 1,000 hides that late-night and foreign charges have much higher fraud rates.
Knowing only 1 in 1,000 charges is fraud doesn't matter once the AI has already flagged a specific transaction.
If fraud is only 1 in 1,000, an AI with 99% accuracy catches fewer than 1 fraud per 100,000 charges.
fix: Treat 1 in 1,000 as 1% when computing the alert counts.
Ignore the 1-in-1,000 background rate once a charge is already flagged.
Split the 1-in-1,000 rate by card tier before running the AI.
Multiply 1 in 1,000 by 99% to get the overall false-alarm rate.

diagnosis: Flagging 99% of real fraud automatically guarantees that 99% of flagged charges are real fraud.
Missing 1% of real fraud on a card network means hundreds of thousands of dollars slip through unflagged.
A 99% catch rate is impossible when only 1 in 1,000 charges is fraud — you can't catch 0.99 of a single charge.
Catching 99% of fraud means only 1% of all alerts can be mistakes.
fix: Raise the catch rate to 100% before trusting any alert.
Test on 100,000 charges so 99% of fraud equals a whole number (99 frauds).
Report how many real frauds were missed per 1,000 charges instead of 99%.
Combine 99% catch rate with 1% false alerts into a single 98% net score.

diagnosis: A 1% false-alert rate on legitimate charges means 1 out of every 100 alerts is wrong, leaving 99% right.
1% false alerts plus 99% catch rate sums to 100%, which proves the two metrics were double-counted.
On 999 legitimate charges, 1% is roughly 100 false alerts, not 10.
A 1% false-alert rate is actually too *low* — legitimate charges should trigger 0% alerts.
fix: Recompute 1% of 999 as ~100 false alerts per 1,000 charges.
Verify that 99% and 1% aren't just complements of the same single metric.
Interpret 1% false alerts as '1% of flagged transactions are innocent'.
Lower the false-alert rate to 0.5% so alerts become 99.5% accurate.

diagnosis: Freezing immediately is fine even at 9% fraud odds because unfreezing takes only a minute.
Agents should freeze only if the customer ignores a confirmation text for 24 hours.
Freezing without pinging the customer violates the 99% accuracy guarantee in line 2.
Even if 99% of alerts were real fraud, freezing accounts still blocks 1 in 100 good customers.
fix: Send an instant SMS/app confirmation before freezing, since ~9 in 10 alerts are legit.
Freeze immediately for 10 minutes, then auto-unfreeze if the customer doesn't reply.
Freeze only when the amount exceeds $1,000 and let smaller alerts pass unverified.
Wait 24 hours for the charge to settle before asking the cardholder.
